title: How would you migrate master data from a legacy system to a custom cloud-based solution (API design, cloud storage, ETL migration, DB setup, monitoring, security, CI/CD)?
shortTitle: How would you migrate master data from a legacy system to a custom cloud-based solution

s1_definition.profdef: A master data migration moves the authoritative reference records of a business, such as customers, accounts, products, and branch details, from an older on-premise system to a newly built cloud platform. It is an ETL pipeline, extract from the legacy source, transform into the new schema while cleaning and validating, and load into the cloud database, executed in controlled phases with reconciliation. Done well it uses staging in cloud object storage, idempotent batch loads, parallel-run validation, strong security over data in transit and at rest, observability on every record, and an automated CI/CD pipeline so the migration tooling itself is tested and repeatable.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India is moving from an old paper-and-mainframe records room to a brand new digital vault in the cloud. The old room holds the master ledgers: every customer like Rajesh and Priya, their account numbers, balances, and KYC details. You cannot just dump the papers into the new vault. You photograph each record (extract), correct smudges and reformat it to the new vault's filing standard (transform), then file it neatly in the new vault (load). You keep the old room open and compare both for a while (parallel run) until you are certain the new vault is perfect, and only then close the old room.
s1_definition.oneliner: Extract, transform, load, reconcile, and parallel-run, treating the migration as idempotent, secure, observable, and automated rather than a one-shot copy.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A master data migration moves the authoritative reference records of a business, such as customers, accounts, products, and branch details, from an older on-premise system to a newly built cloud platform. It is an ETL pipeline, extract from the legacy source, transform into the new schema while cleaning and validating, and load into the cloud database, executed in controlled phases with reconciliation. Done well it uses staging in cloud object storage, idempotent batch loads, parallel-run validation, strong security over data in transit and at rest, observability on every record, and an automated CI/CD pipeline so the migration tooling itself is tested and repeatable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India is moving from an old paper-and-mainframe records room to a brand new digital vault in the cloud. The old room holds the master ledgers: every customer like Rajesh and Priya, their account numbers, balances, and KYC details. You cannot just dump the papers into the new vault. You photograph each record (extract), correct smudges and reformat it to the new vault's filing standard (transform), then file it neatly in the new vault (load). You keep the old room open and compare both for a while (parallel run) until you are certain the new vault is perfect, and only then close the old room.

**One line to remember:** Extract, transform, load, reconcile, and parallel-run, treating the migration as idempotent, secure, observable, and automated rather than a one-shot copy.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with discovery and data profiling. Before moving anything, you profile the legacy data: how many customers, how many accounts, what formats, where the nulls and duplicates and encoding problems are. Legacy systems accumulate decades of dirty data: dates stored as strings, phone numbers in five formats, duplicate customer records. You cannot design the transform until you know the mess you are moving.

Next, schema design in the cloud. You design the target database for the new model, not a mirror of the old one. For master data you often choose a relational database such as Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL or Cloud SQL because master data has strong integrity rules, foreign keys, and needs transactions. You define the tables, constraints, and indexes, and you write the DDL as versioned migrations with a tool like Flyway or Liquibase so the schema is reproducible.

The migration itself is an ETL pipeline. Extract reads from the legacy source, often a nightly database dump, a replica, or change data capture if you need near-real-time. Rather than reading the legacy production database directly under load, you export to cloud object storage first, such as Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage, as the landing and staging zone. Staging in object storage gives you a durable, cheap, replayable copy, so if the load fails you re-run from staging without touching legacy again. Transform cleans, deduplicates, standardizes formats, maps old codes to new codes, and validates each record against business rules such as "balance must be non-negative" and "account must reference a valid customer." Load writes the transformed records into the cloud database in batches.

Idempotency is essential. The load must be safe to run twice, because migrations get interrupted. You achieve this with upserts keyed on a stable natural or legacy key, so re-running updates existing rows rather than creating duplicates. You also checkpoint progress so a restart resumes from the last committed batch rather than from zero.

API design matters because the new cloud platform exposes master data through services. You design clean REST or gRPC APIs such as `GET /api/v1/customers/{id}` and `GET /api/v1/accounts/{id}`, versioned from day one, so consumers migrate off the legacy interfaces onto the new ones. During transition you may run an anti-corruption layer or facade that lets old consumers keep calling familiar endpoints while the data lives in the new store.

Reconciliation and parallel run prove correctness. After loading, you compare counts and checksums: number of customers, sum of balances, record-level hashes between legacy and cloud. You run both systems in parallel, serving reads from the new system while continuing to validate against the old, and you only cut over writes when reconciliation is clean. You always keep a rollback plan.

Security is non-negotiable for banking master data. Data in transit uses TLS. Data at rest is encrypted with KMS-managed keys. Access to staging buckets and the database is least-privilege IAM. Personally identifiable information and KYC fields may be tokenized or masked in non-production environments. Every access is audited.

Monitoring and observability track the migration per record: how many extracted, transformed, loaded, rejected, and why. You emit metrics to Prometheus or CloudWatch, dashboards in Grafana, and alerts when the rejection rate crosses a threshold. A rejected-records table captures every row that failed validation with its reason so operators can fix and replay.

Finally, CI/CD. The migration code, schema migrations, and infrastructure are in version control. A pipeline runs unit tests on the transform logic, runs the schema migrations against a test database, executes a dry run against a sample, and deploys the tooling. The migration is not a hand-run script on someone's laptop; it is a tested, repeatable, automated artifact.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is retiring a thirty-year-old mainframe that holds master data for customers and accounts, including Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), and moving to a cloud platform on AWS.

Problem 1 — the legacy data is dirty. Balances are stored as strings with commas like "1,000,000.00", account statuses use cryptic single letters, and some customer rows are duplicated. If we load this as-is, the new system has wrong balances and duplicate customers. This is why we need a transform step that cleans, parses to BigDecimal, maps codes, and deduplicates before loading.

Problem 2 — the migration got interrupted halfway last time and created duplicates on restart. We re-ran it and loaded Rajesh twice. This is why the load must be idempotent: it upserts on the legacy key, so re-running updates rather than duplicates, and checkpoints so it resumes.

Problem 3 — nobody trusted the new numbers. After the first attempt, finance asked "does the total deposits in the cloud equal the mainframe total?" and we could not answer. This is why we need reconciliation: compare record counts and the sum of all balances between source and target before cutover.

The mini-project builds a runnable ETL demo: a `LegacyRecord` representing raw mainframe rows, an `Extractor` that reads them, a `Transformer` that cleans and validates into a `CustomerAccount`, an idempotent `Loader` simulating upsert into the cloud database, a `RejectedStore` for bad rows, and a `Reconciler` that compares source and target. It migrates Rajesh and Priya plus one dirty duplicate and one invalid row.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Apply schema migrations to the cloud DB first
flyway -url=jdbc:postgresql://aurora-cluster:5432/masterdb migrate

# Run the ETL demo
java -cp target/masterdata-migration-1.0.0.jar com.bank.migration.MigrationDemo

# Dry run against a sample (CI/CD stage)
java -jar target/masterdata-migration-1.0.0.jar --mode=dry-run --sample=1000

# Query migrated data through the new API
curl https://api.nbi-cloud.com/api/v1/customers/CUST01
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four legacy rows. Rajesh (valid), Priya (valid), Rajesh again (duplicate), and a bad row with a negative balance and unknown KYC.

Step 1: Extract reads all four rows from staging. In production these come from an S3 export of the mainframe dump, not the live mainframe.

Step 2: Row 1, Rajesh. Transform splits the pipe-delimited line, maps KYC code V to VERIFIED, type S to SAVINGS, status A to ACTIVE, and parses "1,000,000.00" by stripping the comma into a BigDecimal. All validations pass. Load upserts SAV2001 as an INSERT.

Step 3: Row 2, Priya. Same clean path. Type C maps to CURRENT. Load inserts CUR3001.

Step 4: Row 3, Rajesh duplicate. Transform succeeds identically. Load calls upsert on SAV2001, which already exists, so it becomes an UPDATE, not a second row. This is idempotency in action: the duplicate did not create a duplicate record.

Step 5: Row 4, bad row. Transform parses the balance as negative and throws ValidationException "negative balance not allowed". The loader never sees it. It goes to the RejectedStore with its reason, and a severe log is written.

Step 6: Reconcile computes the source total of unique valid balances (1,000,000 + 250,000 = 1,250,000) and compares it to the loaded total (also 1,250,000). They match, so it logs RECONCILE OK.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] INSERTED SAV2001 (Rajesh Kumar, balance=1000000.00)
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] INSERTED CUR3001 (Priya Sharma, balance=250000.00)
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] UPDATED SAV2001 (Rajesh Kumar, balance=1000000.00)
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [SEVERE ] REJECTED [negative balance not allowed] : CUST03|Bad Row|Unknown|X|ACC9999|S|-500.00|A
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] RECONCILE OK — source total = target total = 1250000.00
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Loaded accounts = 2, rejected = 1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To migrate master data from a legacy system to a custom cloud platform, I treat it as a controlled ETL pipeline with reconciliation and a parallel run, not a one-shot copy. I begin with discovery and data profiling, because legacy systems accumulate decades of dirty data such as balances stored as comma-separated strings, cryptic status codes, and duplicate customer rows, and I cannot design a correct transform until I understand that mess. Then I design the target schema for the new model with proper constraints and versioned migrations using Flyway, so the cloud database is reproducible rather than a blind mirror of the old one.

The pipeline itself extracts from the legacy source into cloud object storage such as S3 as a durable, replayable staging zone, so if a load fails I re-run from staging without ever touching the fragile legacy system again. The transform step cleans, parses amounts into BigDecimal, maps old codes to new codes, deduplicates, and validates each record against business rules like non-negative balances and valid KYC. The load step writes to the cloud database in batches, and critically it is idempotent: it upserts on a stable key and checkpoints progress, so if the migration is interrupted and restarted it updates existing rows instead of creating duplicates. On an earlier attempt we did not have this and a restart loaded Rajesh twice, which is exactly the failure idempotency prevents.

I prove correctness with reconciliation and a parallel run. After loading I compare record counts and the sum of all balances between source and target, and I only trust the migration when the numbers match exactly, which is the answer finance always demands. I keep the old system live, serve reads from the new one while continuously validating against the old, and cut over writes only when reconciliation is clean, always with a rollback plan. I expose the migrated data through clean versioned REST APIs, and during transition I front it with an anti-corruption facade so existing consumers keep working while they migrate.

Security and automation wrap everything. For banking master data I encrypt in transit with TLS and at rest with KMS keys, lock down staging buckets and the database with least-privilege IAM, mask PII in non-production, and audit every access. Observability tracks each record as extracted, transformed, loaded, or rejected, with a rejects table capturing every bad row and its reason so operators can fix and replay, and alerts fire when the rejection rate spikes. The whole migration lives in CI/CD: the transform logic is unit tested, the schema migrations run against a test database, a dry run executes on a sample, and the tooling and infrastructure deploy as versioned, tested artifacts rather than a hand-run script on someone's laptop.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that master data migration is an idempotent, reconciled ETL pipeline that stages in cloud object storage, cleans and validates on the way in, upserts safely so restarts never duplicate, proves itself by matching counts and balance totals between source and target, runs the old and new systems in parallel before cutover, and is fully secured, observed, and automated through CI/CD.

---

keyPoints: Database per service: each microservice owns its data
Idempotency: same request produces same result — safe retries
Eventual consistency: services sync via events, not distributed locks
Shared database anti-pattern: breaks service independence
